note.text: An article helps readers identify what happened and why it matters. A headline identifies focus; a lead presents the central event; later paragraphs develop relevant details and attribute their source. Quote only words supplied in the task and preserve meaning in indirect reports. Do not invent a real witness’s words or present a proposal as completed. This model reports classroom fiction, not current news or a universal examination format.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to separate reported facts, attribution and unconfirmed outcomes in an article. Builds on: directed writing, reported viewpoints and resource reading. Leads to: expository explanation and accurate reporting.

paper_task.prompt: Report the fictional stream discussion in a newspaper-style article. Include headline, lead, attributed details and unknowns. Use supplied facts; invent no real witnesses or direct quotations.
model: Village group seeks guidance on shared stream

A fictional village group proposes seeking technical guidance before changing stream use for a school garden. Members recorded concerns about watering the garden and keeping water clear for existing users.

According to the classroom passage, discussion with affected users is planned. No measured flow or laboratory result is supplied. There is also no permission to alter the stream, so the discussion cannot be reported as an authorised construction project.
Compatibility of the uses in every season remains unestablished. Further information is part of the proposal, rather than an outcome achieved already.
checklist: Focused headline: a heading identifying the central event.
Informative lead: an opening supplying the main event.
Attribution: identification of the information’s source.
Status accuracy: preservation of whether action is planned or completed.
Use relevant original details and check sentence boundaries, agreement and spelling.
